stem: A 3-year-old boy has short upper arms and thighs with a normal-length trunk, a large head with frontal bossing, a low nasal bridge and lumbar lordosis. His legs are straight and his intelligence is normal.
oneliner: 3M + short arms/thighs, normal trunk + big head, frontal bossing, low nasal bridge + lordosis → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **proportionate** short stature; limbs not selectively shortened
whyNot.B: **milder** disproportion with a normal-looking head and face
whyNot.C: **bowed legs** with low mineral labs; legs here are straight
whyNot.D: **fractures and blue sclerae**; none described

why: **Rhizomelic limb shortening with a normal trunk**, macrocephaly with frontal bossing and a low nasal bridge, and lordosis = achondroplasia.

stem: A newborn girl is born to two parents of normal height. She has short upper arms and thighs and a large head, and she breathes without difficulty. Genetic testing shows a single-base gain-of-function mutation in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 gene on chromosome 4.
oneliner: Newborn F + short proximal limbs + big head + normal-height parents + FGFR3 gain-of-function → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **severe respiratory failure**, usually fatal; this infant breathes easily
whyNot.B: **mild** shortening, often not obvious at birth, with a normal head
whyNot.D: **hitchhiker thumb and cystic ears** (SLC26A2); not described
whyNot.E: **collagen defect with fractures**; no FGFR3 mutation

why: **FGFR3 gain-of-function** with short proximal limbs and macrocephaly in a child of normal parents (new mutation) = achondroplasia.

stem: A 7-year-old girl has delayed closure of her fontanelles, a prominent forehead, and extra unerupted teeth on dental films. She can touch her shoulders together in front of her chest. Her height is normal and she has had no fractures.
oneliner: 7F + open sutures + frontal bossing + extra unerupted teeth + shoulders meet in front of chest → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **fractures and blue sclerae**; none here
whyNot.C: **short limbs**; this child has normal height
whyNot.D: **premature loss** of teeth, not extra teeth; clavicles normal
whyNot.E: **short stature, dense bones and fractures**; none here

why: **Hypoplastic or absent clavicles** (shoulders meet), **open sutures** and **supernumerary teeth** = cleidocranial dysplasia (RUNX2).

stem: A newborn boy has a long, narrow head that is elongated from front to back. A hard ridge can be felt along the midline of the skull, and the anterior fontanelle is nearly closed.
oneliner: Newborn M + long narrow head front to back + hard midline ridge + tiny fontanelle → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **flattened one side** of the head with a parallelogram shape; sutures open
whyNot.B: **enlarged head and bulging fontanelle**; head here is narrow
whyNot.C: **macrocephaly** with short limbs; head here is long and narrow
whyNot.E: **wide-open** sutures and fontanelles, not early closure

why: **Premature fusion of the sagittal suture** gives a long, narrow head with a midline ridge and a closed fontanelle.

stem: A 4-month-old boy has pallor, an enlarged liver and spleen, and poor feeding. Radiographs show diffusely dense bones with a thickened skull base. The blood smear shows teardrop cells and nucleated red cells but no blasts.
oneliner: 4M + pallor + hepatosplenomegaly + diffusely dense bones + leukoerythroblastic smear → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **fractures with thin, fragile bones**; these bones are dense
whyNot.C: **widened growth plates and low density**; bones here are dense
whyNot.D: **blasts** in blood and marrow; bones are not diffusely dense
whyNot.E: **short limbs** with normal bone density; no anemia

why: **Diffusely dense bones** with anemia and **extramedullary hematopoiesis** (marrow space crowded out) = osteopetrosis, from failure of osteoclast bone resorption.

stem: A 13-year-old obese boy has had 3 weeks of right knee and thigh pain with a limp. He is afebrile. The knee examination is normal, but internal rotation of the right hip is limited and the leg turns outward when the hip is flexed.
oneliner: 13M + obese + knee/thigh pain + limp + limited hip internal rotation, afebrile → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: typical age **4 to 8** in a **lean, small** child
whyNot.B: **fever and severe pain** on any hip movement; he is afebrile
whyNot.C: **tibial tubercle tenderness**; the hip is normal in that disease
whyNot.D: **back and sacroiliac pain with morning stiffness**; none here

why: An **obese early adolescent** with **knee pain referred from the hip** and **limited internal rotation** = SCFE.

stem: A 13-year-old boy who plays basketball has had 2 months of pain at the front of the upper shin, just below the knee, that worsens with jumping and running. There was no injury and he has no fever. A lateral radiograph of the knee is shown.
oneliner: 13M + basketball + pain at upper front shin with jumping, no trauma + [x-ray] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **hip pain and limited hip rotation**; the knee pain here is local
whyNot.B: **diffuse pain around the patella** with stairs and sitting; tibial tubercle normal on film
whyNot.D: pain at the **lower pole of the patella**; the tubercle would look normal
whyNot.E: **locking and effusion** at the femoral condyle; none here

why: A **fragmented, prominent tibial tubercle** in an active adolescent with pain at patellar tendon insertion = Osgood-Schlatter disease (traction apophysitis).

image.prompt: Lateral radiograph of a knee in an adolescent showing a prominent tibial tuberosity with a small separate bone fragment at the patellar tendon insertion and soft tissue swelling anterior to it.

stem: A 2-year-old girl suddenly stops using her right arm after her father pulled her up by the hand to stop her from falling. She holds the arm straight and turned in, and cries when the elbow is moved. There is no swelling, bruising or fever.
oneliner: 2F + yanked up by the hand + holds arm still, cries with elbow motion + no swelling or fever → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **swelling and deformity** after a fall onto the arm
whyNot.C: **fever and a swollen, warm joint**; neither is present
whyNot.D: **tenderness over the clavicle** after a fall; arm hangs without elbow pain on traction
whyNot.E: **deformed shoulder** after major force; not caused by a gentle pull

why: **Sudden traction on the extended arm** of a toddler with a painful, still arm and **no swelling** = subluxation of the radial head.

stem: A 68-year-old woman has had 2 months of low back pain after lifting a bag of groceries. Her mother had breast cancer. She has tenderness over L2, and a lumbar x-ray shows generalized decreased density of the vertebrae with mild wedging of L2 and no focal lesions. Calcium 9.4 mg/dL, phosphate 3.6 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 70 U/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 34 ng/mL. Serum protein electrophoresis is normal.
oneliner: 68F + back pain after lifting + L2 tenderness + diffuse osteopenia, wedged L2 + normal Ca/PO4/ALP/SPEP → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **monoclonal spike**, anemia and lytic lesions; SPEP normal and no focal lesions
whyNot.B: **focal lytic or blastic lesions** and often high alkaline phosphatase; none here
whyNot.C: **low vitamin D, low phosphate and raised alkaline phosphatase**; all normal
whyNot.E: **radicular leg pain**; x-ray would not show diffuse bone loss

why: **Diffuse bone loss with a vertebral wedge fracture** in a postmenopausal woman and **normal calcium, phosphate, ALP and SPEP** = osteoporosis.

stem: A 58-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years, treated with daily prednisone, breaks his hip after falling from standing height. Radiographs show a femoral neck fracture and thin, pale-looking bones throughout. Calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase are normal, and he has no back stiffness.
oneliner: 58M + RA 15 y on chronic prednisone + hip fracture from standing + diffuse osteopenia + normal Ca/PO4/ALP → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **low phosphate or vitamin D with raised ALP**; labs here are normal
whyNot.B: **markedly raised ALP** and thick, sclerotic bone
whyNot.D: **punched-out lesions, anemia and high calcium or creatinine**; not described
whyNot.E: **sacroiliitis and spine fusion**; no back stiffness here

why: **Fragility fracture, diffuse osteopenia and long-term steroids** with **normal calcium, phosphate and ALP** = osteoporosis.

stem: A 41-year-old woman with a BMI of 17 kg/m2 sustains a vertebral compression fracture after a sneeze. Her mother broke her hip at age 68. She exercises regularly, does not smoke and drinks little alcohol. Calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, PTH and 25-hydroxyvitamin D are normal, and her sclerae are white.
oneliner: 41F + BMI 17 + mother's hip fracture + vertebral fracture from a sneeze + normal labs, white sclerae → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **low vitamin D or phosphate with high ALP**; normal here
whyNot.C: **blue sclerae and fractures since childhood**; sclerae are white
whyNot.D: **high calcium and PTH**; both normal
whyNot.E: **anemia, monoclonal protein and lytic lesions**; none reported

why: **Low body weight and a maternal fragility fracture** with a **low-trauma vertebral fracture** and normal mineral labs = osteoporosis.

stem: A 72-year-old woman breaks her wrist when she trips over a rug. Bone densitometry shows a T-score of -3.1 at the hip and -2.9 at the spine. Calcium is 9.6 mg/dL, phosphate 3.4 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 75 U/L, PTH 40 pg/mL and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 38 ng/mL.
oneliner: 72F + wrist fracture from a trip + T-score -3.1 + normal Ca/PO4/ALP/PTH/vit D → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **low phosphate or vitamin D with high ALP** and defective mineralization; normal here
whyNot.B: **very high ALP** and localized thick bone, not low density everywhere
whyNot.C: **high calcium and PTH**; both normal
whyNot.E: **monoclonal protein and lytic lesions**; none described

why: **T-score below -2.5 with a fragility fracture** and **normal calcium, phosphate, ALP and PTH** = osteoporosis (bone resorption exceeds formation).

stem: An 84-year-old woman dies of pneumonia. She was 12 cm shorter than in her youth and had a stooped back. At autopsy her thoracolumbar spine is sectioned. A photograph of the spine is shown.
oneliner: 84F + height loss + stooped back + autopsy spine [photo] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **punched-out lytic lesions with soft marrow replaced by tumor**; not seen
whyNot.C: **enlarged, dense, thick vertebrae**; these are thin and porous
whyNot.D: **defective mineralization** seen only on histology, usually with bone pain and low vitamin D; the thin, sparse trabeculae here fit bone loss
whyNot.E: **discrete tumor nodules** in the vertebrae; none seen

why: **Thin, porous vertebral bone with wedge compression and kyphosis** in an elderly woman = osteoporosis.

image.prompt: Gross sagittal section of a human thoracolumbar spine at autopsy showing several wedge-shaped, collapsed vertebral bodies with thin, sparse, porous trabecular bone and an exaggerated forward curve (kyphosis).

stem: A 66-year-old man has had chronic mid and low back pain for several years. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 25 years and drinks little alcohol. He has lost 4 cm in height and has an increased thoracic curve. Spinal tenderness is mild and there is no leg weakness, numbness or sphincter problem. Lateral films show diminished height of several vertebral bodies with wedging and thin cortices. Calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and PTH are normal, and urine protein is negative.
oneliner: 66M + smoker 50 pack-y + chronic back pain + 4 cm height loss + kyphosis + wedged thin vertebrae + normal labs → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **leg pain with walking relieved by sitting**; no neurologic symptoms here
whyNot.B: **focal destructive lesions** and often high ALP or calcium; none seen
whyNot.C: **disc-space narrowing and osteophytes** with normal vertebral height
whyNot.D: **proteinuria (Bence Jones) and punched-out lesions**; urine protein negative

why: **Height loss, kyphosis and multiple wedged vertebrae** in a smoker with **normal labs** = osteoporosis (smoking is a risk factor).

stem: A 70-year-old woman who rarely goes outdoors has diffuse bone pain and difficulty rising from a chair. She has tenderness over the shins and a waddling gait. Calcium is 8.0 mg/dL, phosphate 2.2 mg/dL, PTH 120 pg/mL, alkaline phosphatase 260 U/L and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 8 ng/mL.
oneliner: 70F + housebound + diffuse bone pain + proximal weakness + shin tenderness + low Ca, low PO4, high PTH/ALP, low vit D → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **high calcium** with high PTH; calcium here is low
whyNot.B: **normal calcium, phosphate and ALP**; labs here are abnormal
whyNot.D: **focal lesions** and normal PTH and vitamin D
whyNot.E: **low PTH**; PTH here is high

why: **Bone pain, proximal weakness and tender shins** with **low calcium and phosphate, high PTH and ALP and low 25-OH vitamin D** = osteomalacia (adult vitamin D deficiency).

stem: A 14-month-old dark-skinned boy has been breastfed exclusively and has received no vitamin supplements. He has bowed legs, widened wrists and a row of bumps along the costochondral junctions. Calcium is low and PTH and alkaline phosphatase are high.
oneliner: 14M + dark skin + exclusive breastfeeding, no supplement + bowed legs, wide wrists, beaded ribs + low Ca, high PTH/ALP → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **normal calcium and normal PTH** with isolated low phosphate
whyNot.C: **lethargy, constipation and large tongue** with normal bone mineral labs
whyNot.D: **short limbs and large head** with normal calcium and ALP
whyNot.E: **fractures with blue sclerae** and normal calcium, PTH and ALP

why: **Exclusive breastfeeding without supplement, bowed legs, widened wrists and rachitic rosary** with **low calcium and high PTH** = nutritional rickets.

stem: A 3-year-old girl eats a strict vegan diet without supplements and lives far north, where she spends little time in the sun. She has had two fractures after minor falls. Her legs are bowed and her wrists are wide. Her sclerae are white, her teeth are normal, and she has no bruises or bleeding gums. Alkaline phosphatase is high.
oneliner: 3F + vegan, no supplements, little sun + 2 low-trauma fractures + bowed legs + white sclerae + high ALP → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **blue sclerae and abnormal teeth**; sclerae here are white and ALP is normal
whyNot.B: **bleeding gums and perifollicular hemorrhages**; none here
whyNot.C: **bruises and unexplained injuries**; none here, and bones are demineralized
whyNot.E: **low alkaline phosphatase** with early tooth loss; ALP here is high

why: **No dairy or supplements and little sunlight** with **bowed legs, wide wrists and fractures** after minor trauma = rickets.

stem: A 67-year-old man has had dull low back pain for 6 months. A lateral radiograph shows an enlarged lumbar vertebral body with a thickened, sclerotic cortical rim and a lucent center. Calcium is 9.5 mg/dL, phosphate 3.4 mg/dL and alkaline phosphatase 650 U/L. AST and ALT are normal.
oneliner: 67M + low back pain + enlarged vertebra with sclerotic rim + ALP 650 with normal Ca/PO4/liver tests → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **normal ALP** and generalized thin bone; not one enlarged, sclerotic vertebra
whyNot.C: **multiple blastic foci** without enlargement of the bone; a single enlarged vertebra here
whyNot.D: **high calcium and low phosphate**; both normal
whyNot.E: **low phosphate or vitamin D**, and thin, poorly mineralized bone

why: **Isolated high alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium, phosphate and liver tests** and an **enlarged vertebra with a thick sclerotic rim (picture frame)** = Paget disease.

stem: A 62-year-old woman has had a vague, dull ache in the right thigh and hip for several months. A radiograph shows a thickened cortex and coarse trabeculae in the femur, which looks widened. There is no fever or soft-tissue mass. Calcium and phosphate are normal and alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised.
oneliner: 62F + dull thigh/hip ache for months + thick coarse femoral cortex + high ALP, normal Ca/PO4 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **soft-tissue mass and sunburst periosteal reaction**; none here
whyNot.B: **low calcium or phosphate** and thin, pseudofractured bone
whyNot.C: **fever, local warmth** and raised inflammatory markers; absent
whyNot.D: **thin cortices and normal ALP**; cortex here is thick

why: **Thickened, coarse femoral cortex** with **very high ALP and normal calcium and phosphate** in an older adult = Paget disease.

stem: A 48-year-old man with heavy alcohol use for 20 years has progressive right groin pain on walking and reduced hip motion. He is afebrile, and calcium and alkaline phosphatase are normal. Plain radiographs of the hip are normal, but MRI shows a band of low T1 signal in the subchondral femoral head.
oneliner: 48M + heavy alcohol + weight-bearing groin pain + limited motion + normal x-ray, abnormal MRI of femoral head → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

whyNot.A: **fever, acute onset** and an effusion with high WBC; not here
whyNot.B: **very high ALP** and thick, dense bone
whyNot.D: **high calcium** and subperiosteal resorption
whyNot.E: **fever, weight loss** and exposure history; none here

answer: Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of the femoral head
why: **Alcohol use, weight-bearing hip pain** and a **normal x-ray with abnormal MRI** of the femoral head = avascular necrosis.

stem: An 82-year-old woman falls at home and cannot bear weight on her right leg. The leg is shortened and externally rotated. A radiograph shows a fracture line running between the greater and lesser trochanters.
oneliner: 82F + fall at home + cannot bear weight + shortened, externally rotated leg + fracture between trochanters → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: fracture line **through the neck**, proximal to the trochanters
whyNot.B: leg **shortened and internally rotated**, with a high-energy injury
whyNot.C: **groin pain with a stable, normally positioned leg**
whyNot.D: **gradual pain** over years, no fracture line

why: **Shortened, externally rotated leg** after a fall with a **fracture between the trochanters** = intertrochanteric hip fracture.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is restrained in a car that is struck from the side. Her right upper arm is swollen, tender and deformed. A radiograph of the arm is shown.
oneliner: 35F + car crash + swollen, deformed upper arm + [x-ray] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Surgical neck fracture of the humerus

whyNot.A: break at the **proximal humerus** below the tubercles, near the shoulder
whyNot.B: break **just above the elbow**, typical in children
whyNot.D: pain and deformity **over the collarbone**, not the upper arm
whyNot.E: **squared-off shoulder** with the humeral head out of the glenoid

why: A **mid-shaft humeral break** after major trauma with a swollen, angulated upper arm = humeral shaft fracture (radial nerve runs in the spiral groove).

image.prompt: Anteroposterior radiograph of the upper arm showing a transverse fracture through the middle of the humeral shaft with mild angulation and displacement of the fragments.

stem: A 67-year-old woman falls onto her outstretched hand. Her wrist is swollen and bruised, and wrist motion is painful. She is not tender in the anatomical snuffbox. A radiograph of the wrist is shown.
oneliner: 67F + fell on outstretched hand + swollen, bruised wrist + snuffbox not tender + [x-ray]
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **snuffbox tenderness** and a normal-appearing radius; not tender here
whyNot.C: an **isolated small fragment** off the ulna with the radius intact
whyNot.D: a **radial shaft fracture** with distal radioulnar joint disruption
whyNot.E: **volar carpal mass and displaced lunate**; radius intact

why: A **fall on the outstretched hand** in an older woman with a swollen wrist and a **dorsally displaced distal radius fracture** on film = Colles fracture.

image.prompt: Lateral wrist radiograph showing a transverse fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement and angulation of the distal fragment, giving a dinner-fork shape.

stem: A 24-year-old woman falls onto her outstretched hand and has pain and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. The distal radius and the ulnar side of the wrist are not tender.
oneliner: 24F + fell on outstretched hand + anatomical snuffbox tenderness → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **central volar wrist tenderness** with a hard volar mass; snuffbox not tender
whyNot.B: **tenderness and deformity at the distal radius**; not tender here
whyNot.C: **ulnar-side pain** over the hook of the hamate after gripping a club or bat
whyNot.E: **dorsal ulnar-sided wrist pain**, not radial

why: A **fall on an outstretched hand** with **snuffbox tenderness** = scaphoid fracture (risk of avascular necrosis of the proximal pole).

stem: A 30-year-old woman falls onto her outstretched hand. Her wrist is swollen and tender, with a hard mass just proximal to the wrist crease on the palm side. She is tender over the center of the volar wrist, and the anatomical snuffbox is not tender. A lateral wrist radiograph is shown.
oneliner: 30F + fell on outstretched hand + volar wrist mass + central volar tenderness, snuffbox spared + [x-ray]
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **snuffbox tenderness**; here the snuffbox is spared
whyNot.C: **dorsal displacement of the capitate** with the lunate aligned on the radius
whyNot.D: **tenderness at the ulnar volar base of the palm**, no volar carpal mass
whyNot.E: **pain over the hook of the hamate**, ulnar side, with grip

why: A **volar mass with central volar wrist tenderness** and a lunate **tipped and displaced anteriorly** on the lateral film = lunate dislocation.

image.prompt: Lateral wrist radiograph showing the lunate rotated and displaced toward the palm side, tilted like a spilled teacup, with the capitate no longer sitting in the lunate cup.

stem: A 28-year-old man who jogs steps into a hole and his foot is forcibly everted. He has swelling over both sides of the ankle, tenderness over the lateral malleolus and medial ankle, and cannot bear weight. An ankle radiograph is shown.
oneliner: 28M + jogger, foot forced everted + swelling both sides of ankle + cannot bear weight + [x-ray]
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **ligament stretch with a normal x-ray**; the film is abnormal here
whyNot.B: **posterior pain with a gap** and a positive Thompson test, normal bone
whyNot.C: **comminuted distal tibial plafond** after a fall from a height
whyNot.D: **heel pain after axial load** from a fall; the ankle mortise is intact

answer: Ankle fracture (fibular fracture above the syndesmosis)
why: **Forced eversion** with **bilateral ankle swelling** and a **fibular fracture above the tibiofibular joint** with medial injury = ankle fracture.

image.prompt: Anteroposterior ankle radiograph showing an oblique fracture of the distal fibula above the level of the ankle joint with widening of the medial clear space between the medial malleolus and the talus.

stem: A 28-year-old man falls from a ladder onto his left side. He has pain on deep breaths and tenderness over the lower left ribs, and his breathing is shallow. Breath sounds are equal, the chest wall moves normally, and oxygen saturation is 96%. A chest radiograph shows breaks in four adjacent ribs, each at a single site, with fully expanded lungs.
oneliner: 28M + ladder fall + pleuritic left chest pain + shallow breathing + 4 ribs broken at single sites, lungs expanded → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **paradoxical chest wall movement** from segmental fractures; wall moves normally here
whyNot.B: **absent breath sounds** and a visible pleural line; lungs are fully expanded
whyNot.D: **hypoxemia with patchy infiltrates**; oxygen saturation and lung fields are normal
whyNot.E: **no trauma** and no bony break on film

why: **Trauma, pleuritic chest wall pain and four single-site rib breaks** without paradoxical motion or pneumothorax = rib fractures.

stem: A 30-year-old man is struck in the right eye by a baseball. He has double vision on looking up, limited upward gaze of the right eye, and numbness of the cheek below the eye. The cheekbone contour is normal and he opens his mouth fully; there is no proptosis, his visual acuity is normal and his bite is normal.
oneliner: 30M + baseball to eye + diplopia and limited upgaze + infraorbital numbness + normal cheek contour, bite and acuity → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **flattened cheek and trismus** from fractures at several buttresses; cheek and mouth opening are normal
whyNot.C: **mobile midface and malocclusion**; his bite is normal
whyNot.D: **proptosis and falling vision**; neither is present
whyNot.E: **loss of vision and a deformed globe**; acuity is normal

why: **Limited upgaze with diplopia** (inferior rectus entrapment) and **infraorbital numbness** after a blow to the orbit = orbital floor blowout fracture.

stem: A 25-year-old man bites into a large burger and now cannot close his mouth. He is drooling and has pain in front of both ears, with a visible hollow in each preauricular area. There was no blow to the face and his bite was normal before.
oneliner: 25M + bit a big burger + mouth stuck open + drooling + preauricular hollows, no trauma → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **blow to the face**, malocclusion and a step-off; no trauma here
whyNot.B: **clicking and pain** but the mouth can still be closed
whyNot.C: **antipsychotic or antiemetic exposure** with tongue and neck spasm; none here
whyNot.E: **trismus (jaw cannot open)** with spasms, the opposite problem

why: **Mouth locked open** after wide opening, with drooling and **preauricular hollows**, = bilateral anterior TMJ dislocation.

stem: A 45-year-old woman started an overhead weight-lifting program 3 weeks ago and now has right shoulder pain. She is tender just lateral to the acromion and has pain and weakness on resisted abduction. Passive range of motion is full, and her arm drops when it is held abducted to 90 degrees.
oneliner: 45F + new overhead lifting + tender lateral to acromion + weak resisted abduction + full passive ROM + drop arm → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **global loss of passive motion**; passive range here is full
whyNot.C: **bicipital groove tenderness** with pain on resisted supination or flexion
whyNot.D: **painful arc** without weakness or an arm that drops
whyNot.E: **squared shoulder after trauma**, not gradual overuse

why: **Pain and weakness on resisted abduction** with full passive motion and a **positive drop-arm test** = supraspinatus rotator cuff tear.

stem: A 28-year-old man who lifts weights feels a pop in the front of his elbow while lifting a heavy dumbbell. There is swelling and bruising over the antecubital fossa. Elbow flexion and forearm supination are weak, but pronation, wrist extension and sensation are normal.
oneliner: 28M + pop in front of elbow lifting + antecubital swelling and bruising + weak flexion and supination → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **flexion weakness with preserved supination**; supination is weak here
whyNot.B: **wrist drop and sensory loss** over the dorsal hand; extension is normal
whyNot.C: **pain and weakness with pronation**; pronation is normal
whyNot.D: **shoulder deformity**, not antecubital bruising

why: **A pop in the antecubital fossa with weak supination and flexion** after a heavy lift = distal biceps tendon rupture.

stem: A 20-year-old man playing football catches his ring fingertip on an opponent's jersey as he pulls away, and he feels a pop at the tip of the finger. When he makes a fist, the fingertip stays extended. He cannot flex the distal joint when the proximal joint is held still.
oneliner: 20M + football, ring fingertip caught on jersey + pop + cannot flex DIP → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **cannot extend** the DIP after a ball hits the tip; flexion intact
whyNot.B: **PIP flexed and DIP hyperextended**, from central slip injury
whyNot.D: **painful catching or locking** with no acute injury or lost flexion
whyNot.E: **lost PIP flexion** while DIP flexion is preserved

why: **Forced extension of a flexed fingertip** and **loss of DIP flexion** with other joints held still = FDP tendon avulsion.

stem: A 36-year-old woman who plays tennis has had 7 months of pain on the thumb side of the wrist. The pain is worse with gripping and lifting her child, and there is no numbness or injury. She is tender over the radial styloid, and pain is reproduced when the thumb is tucked in the fist and the wrist is bent toward the ulna.
oneliner: 36F + tennis + 7 mo radial wrist pain with grip + tender radial styloid + pain on thumb-in-fist ulnar deviation → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **fall with snuffbox tenderness**; no injury here
whyNot.C: **pain at the thumb base** with a positive grind test
whyNot.D: **numbness in the median nerve distribution**; none here
whyNot.E: **swelling and crepitus on the dorsal forearm**, several cm proximal to the wrist

why: **Radial styloid tenderness** and pain on **thumb-tucked ulnar deviation** (Finkelstein) = tenosynovitis of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.

stem: A 24-year-old man strikes his flexed right knee against the dashboard in a car crash. With the knee at 90 degrees, the tibia sags backward and moves excessively posteriorly when pushed. The anterior drawer test, Lachman test, and varus and valgus stress tests are normal.

whyNot.A: **anterior** tibial translation and a positive Lachman test; Lachman normal here

why: **Posterior tibial sag and positive posterior drawer** after a dashboard injury with other tests normal = PCL injury.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has had 6 weeks of pain over the outer right hip, worse on waking and when lying on that side. She is tender over the greater trochanter. Passive hip rotation is painless and sensation over the lateral thigh is normal.
oneliner: 52F + 6 wk lateral hip pain + worse lying on side + tender greater trochanter + painless hip rotation → ?

whyNot.E: **shooting leg pain with a positive straight leg raise**; not described

why: **Lateral hip pain worse lying on the side** with **greater trochanter tenderness** and a normal hip joint = trochanteric bursitis.

stem: A 25-year-old man who rides horses regularly has had a painful swelling of the inner thigh for 3 weeks after repeated blows from the saddle. The mass has become firm and well circumscribed. There is no fever or skin change, and a radiograph shows a rim of calcification around the mass.

whyNot.B: **steadily growing mass with central, not peripheral, calcification** and no trauma link

whyNot.E: **bruit or thrill** over a pulsatile mass; none described

why: **Repeated muscle trauma** followed by a **firm, circumscribed mass with a calcified rim** = heterotopic bone formation in muscle.

stem: A 16-year-old girl has had brief, sharp pain on the left side of the chest for 2 days. Pressing on the fourth costal cartilage reproduces the pain exactly. The pain does not change with position, there was no injury, and she has no fever. The lung and heart examinations, ECG and chest film are normal.
oneliner: 16F + sharp left chest pain + reproduced by pressing on 4th costal cartilage + normal ECG/film, no trauma → ?

stem: An 8-year-old boy has a plaster cast removed after 3 weeks for forearm fractures. The forearm is thinner than the other side. Reflexes and sensation are normal, there are no fasciculations, and creatine kinase is normal. A muscle biopsy shows small fibers, mainly type 2, with no fiber-type grouping, necrosis or inflammation.
oneliner: 8M + forearm cast 3 wk + thinner forearm + normal reflexes/sensation/CK + type 2 fiber atrophy, no grouping → ?

why: **Immobilization** with a smaller limb, **normal nerve function and CK**, and **type 2 fiber atrophy without grouping** = disuse atrophy.

stem: A 40-year-old man has a humeral shaft fracture repaired and placed in a cast. Afterward he cannot extend his wrist or fingers and has numbness over the back of the hand and first web space. Elbow flexion, finger abduction and thumb opposition are normal.
oneliner: 40M + humerus fracture repair + wrist drop + numb dorsal hand/first web space + normal flexion, abduction, opposition → ?

whyNot.C: **weak elbow flexion** and numbness of the lateral forearm
whyNot.D: **weak thumb opposition** and loss of palmar sensation

why: **Wrist drop with dorsal hand numbness** after a humeral shaft injury (nerve in the spiral groove) = radial nerve injury.

stem: A 55-year-old man has pelvic lymph node dissection for prostate cancer. Afterward his right leg swings outward when he walks and he cannot cross it over the other leg. Thigh adduction is weak and there is numbness of the medial thigh. Knee extension and hip abduction are normal.

whyNot.B: **weak knee extension** and loss of the patellar reflex
whyNot.D: **foot drop** with lateral leg numbness

stem: A 30-year-old man has a deep forearm laceration. He cannot flex the distal joint of his index finger when the middle joint is held straight, but he can flex the middle joint.
oneliner: 30M + forearm laceration + cannot flex index DIP with PIP held extended, PIP flexion intact → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **lost PIP flexion** with DIP flexion intact
whyNot.C: **weak MCP flexion with IP extension**, not DIP flexion
whyNot.D: **weak finger abduction and adduction**
whyNot.E: **cannot extend** the MCP, flexion intact

why: **Lost isolated DIP flexion** with PIP flexion preserved = flexor digitorum profundus injury.

stem: A 45-year-old woman who types all day wakes at night with numbness and tingling in her thumb, index and middle fingers, which improve when she shakes her hand. Tapping over the volar wrist reproduces the tingling.
oneliner: 45F + typist + night numbness thumb/index/middle fingers + relieved by shaking + Tinel positive → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **neck pain radiating down the arm** that worsens with neck movement

stem: A 38-year-old woman has aching and numbness along the ulnar side of her left forearm and hand, worse when she lifts her arms overhead. A chest radiograph shows a complete cervical rib, and CT shows the lower trunk of the brachial plexus draped over it. She has no Horner syndrome and the lung apices are clear.
oneliner: 38F + ulnar-side arm numbness/pain worse overhead + cervical rib + plexus compression on CT + no Horner → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.D: **Horner syndrome and an apical mass**; absent here
whyNot.E: **local elbow tenderness** and no cervical rib or plexus compression

why: A **cervical rib compressing the lower brachial plexus** with ulnar-side symptoms on overhead use = thoracic outlet syndrome.

stem: A 28-year-old man feels sudden low back pain while lifting a heavy box, with pain shooting down the back of the left leg to the foot. Raising the straightened left leg reproduces the pain, and there was no fall.
oneliner: 28M + sudden back pain lifting heavy box + pain shooting down one leg + positive straight leg raise → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **localized paraspinal pain** that does not radiate below the knee
whyNot.C: **older patient with pain on walking** relieved by flexion

why: **Sudden back pain with lifting and radicular pain down one leg** with a positive straight leg raise = lumbar disc herniation.

stem: A 45-year-old man has had 3 weeks of low back pain with tenderness of the lumbar spine, and now cannot dorsiflex his left foot. He has no saddle numbness, bladder or bowel problems, and sensation over the lateral leg is only mildly reduced. MRI shows a disc fragment protruding posterolaterally into the spinal canal at L4-L5.
oneliner: 45M + 3 wk back pain + spinal tenderness + left foot drop + no saddle/bladder symptoms + disc fragment into canal L4-L5 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **leg pain on walking relieved by sitting** with narrowed canal from bony overgrowth
whyNot.B: **forward slip of one vertebra** with a step-off on film
whyNot.D: **saddle anesthesia and bladder or bowel dysfunction**; absent
whyNot.E: **foot drop without back pain**, and no disc fragment on MRI

why: **Back pain with foot drop** and an MRI showing a **disc fragment protruding into the canal** = lumbar disc herniation (L5 root).

stem: A 68-year-old woman has had years of painful hands, and now has trouble buttoning her coat. Morning stiffness lasts about 10 minutes. She has no rash or nail changes. A photograph of her hands is shown.
oneliner: 68F + years of painful hands + trouble buttoning + stiffness 10 min + no rash or nail change + [photo]
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **MCP and PIP swelling with long morning stiffness**; distal joints and bony nodules point away
whyNot.C: **nail pitting and dactylitis**; no skin or nail changes
whyNot.D: **yellow-white tophi** and acute attacks
whyNot.E: **acute knee or wrist attacks** with chondrocalcinosis, not nodules

image.prompt: Photograph of both hands of an older woman showing hard bony nodules at the distal interphalangeal joints and similar nodules at the proximal interphalangeal joints, with the knuckle joints and wrists looking normal and no skin or nail changes.

stem: A 56-year-old obese woman with type 2 diabetes has right knee pain that worsens after walking and by evening. Morning stiffness lasts 10 minutes, and low-dose ibuprofen helps only partly. The knee has bony enlargement and crepitus without warmth or redness, and she is afebrile. A radiograph shows joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes.

whyNot.C: **fever and a hot, effusive joint**; she is afebrile
whyNot.E: **acute attacks with chondrocalcinosis**, not gradual use-related pain

why: **Pain worse with use, brief stiffness, crepitus** and **joint space narrowing with osteophytes and sclerosis** = osteoarthritis.

stem: A 72-year-old man has bilateral hip pain that worsens through the day, with 5 minutes of morning stiffness. Biopsy of articular cartilage shows surface fibrillation, clusters of chondrocytes and loss of proteoglycan matrix, without pannus.
oneliner: 72M + hip pain worse by day + stiffness 5 min + cartilage fibrillation, chondrocyte clusters, matrix loss, no pannus → ?

stem: A 29-year-old woman has had 3 months of swelling and pain in the PIP and MCP joints of both hands, with 2 hours of morning stiffness. The DIP joints are spared and there is no rash or nail change. Rheumatoid factor is positive, anti-CCP antibodies are positive, ESR is 52 mm/h and ANA is negative. oneliner: 29F + 3 mo symmetric PIP/MCP swelling + stiffness 2 h + DIP spared + RF/anti-CCP positive + marginal erosions → ?

stem: A 55-year-old woman has had 12 years of hand pain and stiffness and has trouble buttoning her blouse. Her fingers show hyperextended PIP joints with flexed DIP joints and ulnar deviation at the MCP joints. Rheumatoid factor is positive and radiographs show marginal erosions.

why: **Swan-neck deformities and ulnar deviation** with **RF positivity and marginal erosions** = longstanding rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with 20 years of deforming, symmetric joint disease has fatigue, low-grade fevers and recurrent skin infections. She has no rash. Her white cell count is 2,800/uL with an absolute neutrophil count of 800/uL. A CT of the abdomen is shown.

stem: A 48-year-old man wakes at night with severe pain, redness and swelling of the left great toe. He has had similar episodes before. He eats a normal diet and takes no medicines. stem: A 55-year-old man has had repeated sudden attacks of a hot, red, swollen knee or ankle over the past 3 years. He now has painless lumps on several fingers. A photograph of his hand is shown.

stem: A 58-year-old man has had three episodes in 2 years of sudden severe pain, redness and swelling of the right great toe, each lasting about a week. stem: A 60-year-old obese woman with diabetes has had 1 day of severe pain, redness and warmth of her right knee, with a temperature of 38.6 C. The aspirated fluid is cloudy and yellow, with 85,000 white cells/uL, mostly neutrophils, and no crystals on microscopy.

stem: A 22-year-old man has had 8 months of low back pain and morning stiffness that improve with exercise. Radiographs show bilateral sacroiliitis, and he has no psoriasis, nail changes or urethritis.

stem: A 40-year-old woman has had 8 months of widespread muscle pain, fatigue and unrefreshing sleep, with many tender points on examination. Her ESR, creatine kinase and TSH are normal.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has difficulty climbing stairs and pushes on his thighs to stand up from the floor. His calves are enlarged and firm. Creatine kinase is 18,000 U/L. His mother's brother needed a wheelchair by age 12.

stem: A 9-year-old girl has proximal leg weakness, enlarged calves and difficulty climbing stairs. Her brother had the same calf enlargement and lost the ability to walk at age 10. Her identical twin sister is healthy. Her karyotype is 46,XX and creatine kinase is 1,800 U/L.

stem: A 22-year-old woman has muscle pain and cramps within minutes of exercise, and dark urine afterward. Pain eases and she can continue after a short rest. On a forearm ischemic exercise test, venous lactate does not rise but ammonia does. Muscle biopsy shows subsarcolemmal PAS-positive deposits.

stem: A 20-year-old man who is a sprinter wakes with severe leg weakness after a carbohydrate-rich dinner following a hard training day. His serum potassium is 2.4 mEq/L, and strength returns to normal over several hours. His father had similar attacks, and his thyroid tests are normal.

stem: A 62-year-old man with diabetes, on simvastatin, recently started gemfibrozil. He now has severe muscle pain, weakness and dark urine. Creatine kinase is 28,000 U/L, the urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, and microscopy shows no red cells. TSH is normal.

stem: A 24-year-old man has a closed fracture of the proximal tibia. Two days later he has a tense, swollen leg with severe pain on passive stretch and paresthesias. He then passes dark brown urine and his urine output falls to 200 mL/day. The dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows only 0 to 2 red cells per high-power field. stem: A 14-year-old boy has had 2 months of right knee pain that wakes him at night. A radiograph shows a destructive lesion of the distal femur that elevates the periosteum. Biopsy shows pleomorphic cells producing pink osteoid.

stem: An 11-year-old boy has had 6 weeks of right thigh pain and low-grade fever. A radiograph shows a permeative lytic lesion in the mid-shaft of the femur with layered, onion-skin periosteal new bone. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells with scant cytoplasm, and cultures are negative.

stem: A 52-year-old man who runs has had months of deep thigh pain. A radiograph shows a thickened femoral cortex, and a resected lesion is a glistening, gray-white, lobulated mass. A section of the tumor is shown.

whyNot.D: **herringbone spindle cells** without fat

why: **Deep infiltrating fatty mass with lipoblasts and mitoses** = liposarcoma.

stem: A 55-year-old man has had 4 months of progressive pain and swelling in the right anterior thigh. He has had no injury, and the area is not warm or red. An MRI of the thigh is shown.
oneliner: 55M + 4 mo progressive anterior thigh pain and swelling + no trauma, not warm + [MRI]
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **recent trauma** and shrinking over weeks
whyNot.B: **preceding trauma** and peripheral calcification
whyNot.C: **mass arising from bone** with periosteal reaction
whyNot.D: **fever, warmth and erythema**; not present

why: **A growing, deep, T2-bright muscle mass without trauma or inflammation** = soft tissue sarcoma.
